title: FTD access control with FMC
blurb: Build an access control policy in the Firewall Management Center with intrusion and malware inspection.
scenario: The branch is moving from the ASA to **Cisco Secure Firewall Threat Defense (FTD)**, managed by the **Firewall Management Center (FMC)**. Build the access control policy: inside users may browse the web, with intrusion prevention and malware blocking applied. Block known-bad destinations, and deny everything else.
topology:
Inside zone ── [FTD] ── Outside zone
                 ↑ managed by FMC
objectives: Know the order FTD applies its policies in
Create the access control policy and its default action
Write an allow rule with intrusion and file policies
Choose between Trust and Allow, and remember to deploy

steps.title: The order of inspection
steps.learn: FTD applies its policies in a fixed order. Cheap, early decisions (prefilter and Security Intelligence) spare the deeper engines from work they don't need to do.
steps.task: Put the policies in the order a new connection meets them.
steps.question: Order from first to last.
steps.hint: Fastpath and blocklists come first, then decryption, then working out the user, then rules, and deep inspection last.
items: Prefilter policy (fastpath or block by simple header fields)
Security Intelligence (IP, URL and DNS blocklists)

steps.title: Create the policy
steps.learn: The **default action** handles traffic that matches no rule. **Block all traffic** gives a default deny. The alternative, an intrusion-prevention default, lets unmatched traffic through with inspection.
steps.task: Create policy **Branch-ACP** with the default action **Block all traffic**.
steps.screen: FMC › Policies › Access Control › New Policy

steps.title: Turn on Security Intelligence
steps.learn: **Security Intelligence** drops traffic to and from addresses, URLs and domains that Talos rates as malicious, before any rule is checked.
steps.task: On the Security Intelligence tab, **block** the Talos **Malware**, **Phishing** and **Command and Control** feeds for both networks and URLs.

steps.title: Allow web browsing with inspection
steps.learn: An **Allow** rule passes matching traffic on to deep inspection. Attach an **intrusion policy** (Snort rules) and a **file policy** (Secure Malware Analytics and AMP file reputation) to inspect it. Log at the end of the connection to get the full byte counts.
steps.task: Add rule **Allow-Web**: action **Allow**, from zone **Inside** to zone **Outside**, applications **HTTP and HTTPS**, intrusion policy **Balanced Security and Connectivity**, file policy **Block-Malware**, logging **at end of connection**.

steps.title: Trust or Allow?
steps.question: A colleague suggests changing Allow-Web to **Trust** "to make it faster". What would change?

options.text: Trusted traffic skips the intrusion and file inspection, so the IPS and malware blocking would stop protecting web browsing.
Nothing. Trust and Allow are the same action.
options.why: Trust passes traffic without deep inspection. Allow passes it on to the intrusion and file policies.
Trust only passes traffic. It never blocks.

steps.title: Make it live
steps.question: You saved the policy in FMC. Is it protecting traffic yet?

options.text: No. Changes take effect only after you deploy them to the FTD device (Deploy › Deployment).
Yes. FMC pushes every saved change immediately.
options.why: FMC stages changes until you deploy, so you can review them and deploy everything together.

summary: A Branch-ACP access control policy with a default block, Security Intelligence feeds blocking malware, phishing and CnC, and an Allow-Web rule with intrusion and file inspection and end-of-connection logging, ready to deploy from FMC.
